s2-l001-parallax-magnitude-scale.prompt: Star A has apparent magnitude $m=2$ and star B has $m=7$. Which statement is correct?
options: B appears 100 times brighter than A, since larger magnitudes mean brighter.
A appears 5 times brighter than B, since the magnitude difference is 5.
A appears 100 times brighter than B.
A appears $10^5$ times brighter than B, since magnitudes are logarithmic base 10.
s2-l001-parallax-magnitude-scale.explanation: $m_1-m_2=-2.5\log_{10}(F_1/F_2)$, so $\Delta m=5$ gives $F_1/F_2=10^{2}=100$. The scale is historical (Hipparchus) and runs backward: brighter stars have smaller $m$.

s2-l001-parallax-magnitude-scale.prompt: A star has a parallax of 0.25 arcsec. Compute its distance in light-years (take 1 pc = 3.26 ly).
Explain in your own words why the parallax method works only for relatively nearby stars, and why astronomers measure brightness on a logarithmic (magnitude) scale.
s2-l001-parallax-magnitude-scale.rubric: Full credit requires: parallax angle p = 1/d(pc) shrinks with distance until it is below the measurement precision; so only nearby stars can be measured this way; the eye and stellar fluxes span many orders of magnitude, so a logarithmic scale compresses the range (5 mag = factor 100).
s2-l001-parallax-magnitude-scale.modelAnswer: Parallax is the tiny apparent shift of a star against distant background stars as Earth orbits the Sun; it scales as $1/d$, so beyond some distance it drops below what instruments can resolve. Stellar fluxes span many orders of magnitude (and the eye responds roughly logarithmically), so the magnitude scale is logarithmic: 5 magnitudes is exactly a factor of 100 in flux.

s2-l002-distance-modulus-luminosity.prompt: A star has apparent magnitude $m$ and absolute magnitude $M$ with $m-M<0$. What does this tell you about its distance?
options: It is closer than 10 pc: $M$ is the magnitude it would have at 10 pc, and it looks brighter than that.
It is farther than 10 pc, because it looks brighter than its absolute value, so its light has travelled a long way.
It is exactly 10 pc away, because $m$ and $M$ differ only when the distance is not 10 pc.
Nothing: the distance cannot be inferred from magnitudes alone without a parallax measurement.
s2-l002-distance-modulus-luminosity.explanation: $m-M=5\log_{10}(d/10\ {\rm pc})$ is negative only if $d<10$ pc. The absolute magnitude removes the inverse-square dimming so luminosities can be compared.

s2-l002-distance-modulus-luminosity.prompt: Two stars appear equally bright, but star B is three times farther away than star A. How do their luminosities compare?
options: B is three times more luminous than A.
B is one third as luminous as A.
They have equal luminosity since they look equally bright.
B is nine times more luminous than A.

s2-l002-distance-modulus-luminosity.prompt: A star has apparent magnitude $m=7.2$ and absolute magnitude $M=-0.3$. Using $m-M=5\log_{10}(d/10\ {\rm pc})$, compute its distance in parsecs.
Explain how you would determine a star's luminosity if you could measure its parallax and its apparent brightness, and why astronomers need both.
s2-l002-distance-modulus-luminosity.rubric: Full credit requires: parallax gives distance d; apparent brightness gives flux F; luminosity from L = 4 pi d^2 F (or via distance modulus to absolute magnitude); brightness alone confuses a near faint star with a far luminous one.
s2-l002-distance-modulus-luminosity.modelAnswer: The parallax angle gives the distance, $d=1/p$ (pc). The measured flux $F$ then gives the luminosity from the inverse-square law, $L=4\pi d^2F$. Brightness alone cannot separate a faint nearby star from a luminous distant one, so a distance is needed to turn flux into an intrinsic property.

s2-l003-planck-law-wien-displacement.prompt: A cool red star (3500 K) and a hot blue star (14000 K) are compared. By Wien's law, how do their peak wavelengths compare?
options: The blue star's emission peaks at four times the red star's wavelength.
The blue star's emission peaks at one quarter of the red star's wavelength.
They peak at the same wavelength; only the total power differs.
The blue star's emission peaks at one sixteenth the wavelength, since $\lambda_{\max}\propto1/T^4$.
s2-l003-planck-law-wien-displacement.explanation: $\lambda_{\max}T=2.898\times10^{-3}$ m K, so temperature up by 4 means wavelength down by 4. The $T^4$ law applies to total power, not to the peak position.

s2-l003-planck-law-wien-displacement.prompt: A piece of iron is heated in a forge and glows dull red, then orange, then white-hot. What is the physical origin of this sequence?
options: The iron changes its chemical composition as it heats, so it starts emitting at new atomic lines.
Hotter metal emits only light at its peak wavelength, so the colour jumps from red to orange to white.
The Planck peak moves to shorter wavelength as $T$ rises, so more blue and green light is added to the red.
The total power rises as $T^4$ while the shape of the spectrum stays fixed, so only brightness changes.
s2-l003-planck-law-wien-displacement.explanation: Wien's law $\lambda_{\max}\propto1/T$ shifts the whole continuous Planck curve toward the blue; white means all visible wavelengths are present. The same physics governs the glowing filament of an IR spectrometer source.

s2-l003-planck-law-wien-displacement.prompt: Using $\lambda_{\max}T=2.898\times10^{-3}$ m K, compute the peak wavelength of the Sun's spectrum (effective temperature 5772 K) in nm.
s2-l003-planck-law-wien-displacement.explanation: $\lambda_{\max}=2.898\times10^{-3}/5772=5.02\times10^{-7}$ m $=502$ nm, in the green-blue part of the visible band.

s2-l003-planck-law-wien-displacement.prompt: Explain how Planck's idea of energy quantisation removes the 'ultraviolet catastrophe' of classical blackbody radiation.
s2-l003-planck-law-wien-displacement.rubric: Full credit requires: classical equipartition gives kT to every mode and infinitely many high-frequency modes so intensity grows without bound; quantisation E = h nu means modes with h nu >> kT are rarely excited (exponentially suppressed by Boltzmann factor), cutting off the spectrum at high frequency; resulting peak ~ kT/h.
s2-l003-planck-law-wien-displacement.modelAnswer:
Classically every mode of the radiation field gets energy $kT$, and there are ever more high-frequency modes, so the predicted intensity diverges in the ultraviolet. If energy comes in quanta $h
u$, modes with $h
u\gg kT$ are almost never excited (a Boltzmann factor $e^{-h
u/kT}$), so the spectrum is cut off at high frequency and peaks near $
u\sim kT/h$, as observed.

s2-l004-stefan-boltzmann-color-index.prompt: Red giants are cool ($T_{\rm eff}\sim3500$ K) yet some are far more luminous than the Sun. How is that possible?
options: Cooler stars radiate more per unit area, so cooler means brighter, as for a cooling ember.
$L=4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$: a huge radius (tens to hundreds of solar radii) more than compensates for the lower surface flux.
Red light is more energetic than blue light, so red stars have more luminosity per photon and therefore per unit area of surface.
Their luminosity does not follow the Stefan-Boltzmann law, because their atmospheres are not blackbodies.
s2-l004-stefan-boltzmann-color-index.explanation: Surface flux $\sigma T^4$ falls steeply with falling $T$, but emitting area grows as $R^2$. On the HR diagram red giants sit in the upper right.

s2-l004-stefan-boltzmann-color-index.prompt: The $B-V$ colour index of a star is the same whether the star is nearby or far away (ignoring dust). Why?
options: Because blue and visible light travel at the same speed, so they arrive in step from any distance.
Because colour is a property of the observer's eye and not of the star, so it cannot depend on distance, temperature or anything else.
Because distant stars are always hotter, which exactly offsets their dimming in the blue band.
It is a ratio of fluxes in two bands, and the inverse-square dimming is the same in both bands, so it cancels.
s2-l004-stefan-boltzmann-color-index.explanation: $B-V=-2.5\log(F_B/F_V)+{\rm const}$: the distance factor cancels, leaving a measure of the spectrum's shape, hence of the temperature.

s2-l004-stefan-boltzmann-color-index.prompt: A supergiant has luminosity $L=10^5L_\odot$ and effective temperature $T_{\rm eff}=3500$ K. Using $L=4\pi R^2\sigma T_{\rm eff}^4$, compute its radius in solar radii.
Explain how you could estimate a star's radius if you could only measure its luminosity and its colour (B-V).
s2-l004-stefan-boltzmann-color-index.rubric: Full credit requires: colour index gives effective temperature (Planck shape, via Wien/blackbody); Stefan-Boltzmann L = 4 pi R^2 sigma T^4 then gives R = sqrt(L / 4 pi sigma T^4); a cool star needs a large R to reach the same L.
s2-l004-stefan-boltzmann-color-index.modelAnswer: The $B-V$ colour tells me the shape of the spectrum, hence the effective temperature $T_{\rm eff}$ (cooler is redder). The Stefan-Boltzmann law $L=4\pi R^2\sigma T_{\rm eff}^4$ then fixes the radius, $R=\sqrt{L/(4\pi\sigma T_{\rm eff}^4)}$: for a given luminosity, a cooler star must be larger.

s2-l005-spectral-lines-boltzmann.prompt: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in a 3000 K star, yet its Balmer absorption lines are very weak. Why?
options: Almost all hydrogen atoms are in the ground state ($n=1$).
Hydrogen is almost entirely ionised, leaving no atoms to absorb.
Cool stars do not contain hydrogen.
The Balmer lines are produced only in emission in cool stars.
s2-l005-spectral-lines-boltzmann.explanation: Balmer absorption requires atoms in $n=2$. At 3000 K, $kT\approx0.26$ eV versus a 10.2 eV excitation energy, so the $n=2$ population is negligible (and molecules like TiO dominate the spectrum).

s2-l005-spectral-lines-boltzmann.prompt: Compute the wavelength of the first Balmer line (H$\alpha$, $n_u=3\to n_l=2$) from the Rydberg formula with $R_H=1.0974\times10^7$ m$^{-1}$, in nm.

At $T=10{,}000$ K, compute the Boltzmann population ratio $N_2/N_1$ for the $n=2$ and $n=1$ levels of hydrogen, with degeneracies $g_1=2$, $g_2=8$ and excitation energy 10.2 eV. Give the answer in units of $10^{-5}$.
s2-l005-spectral-lines-boltzmann.explanation: $N_2/N_1=4e^{-10.2/(kT)}$ with $kT=0.8617$ eV, so $4e^{-11.84}=2.9\times10^{-5}$: a tiny fraction, yet the atmosphere contains so many atoms that even this tiny fraction produces strong lines.

s2-l005-spectral-lines-boltzmann.prompt: Explain what produces an absorption line in a star's spectrum, and why the strength of a given line depends on the temperature of the atmosphere through the Boltzmann factor.
s2-l005-spectral-lines-boltzmann.rubric: Full credit requires: a photon is absorbed in a bound-bound transition between levels of an atom, removing that wavelength from the continuum; the line needs atoms already in the lower level; the Boltzmann factor e^(-DeltaE/kT) sets the fraction in that level, rising with T.
s2-l005-spectral-lines-boltzmann.modelAnswer: An absorption line forms when atoms in the cooler atmosphere absorb continuum photons whose energy matches a transition between two bound levels. The strength depends on how many atoms are already in the lower level, which the Boltzmann factor $e^{-\Delta E/kT}$ sets: the excited fraction rises steeply with temperature, exactly as for populations of excited states in a molecular spectrum.

s2-l006-saha-ionization-hr-diagram.prompt: On the HR diagram, where are white dwarfs found, and why?
options: At the upper right: cool but very luminous, so they must be huge.
On the main sequence, at the same luminosity as the Sun.
At the lower left: hot (blue-white) but very faint.
At the upper left: hot and luminous, so they are massive.
s2-l006-saha-ionization-hr-diagram.explanation: HR diagram: temperature increases to the left, luminosity upward. Low $L$ with high $T$ requires small $R$.

s2-l006-saha-ionization-hr-diagram.prompt: Explain why Balmer lines peak in strength near 10,000 K (A stars) rather than in the hottest stars. Use the ideas of excitation (Boltzmann) and ionisation (Saha).
s2-l006-saha-ionization-hr-diagram.rubric: Full credit requires: Balmer absorption needs atoms in n=2: Boltzmann excitation increases with T; but at higher T hydrogen is ionised (Saha), leaving few neutral atoms; product of n=2 fraction and neutral fraction peaks near 10,000 K; ionisation is like a gas-phase equilibrium constant favouring products at high T.
s2-l006-saha-ionization-hr-diagram.modelAnswer: Balmer absorption needs neutral hydrogen atoms in $n=2$. Heating increases the $n=2$ population (Boltzmann), but at higher temperature the Saha equation (a gas-phase ionisation equilibrium) shifts H $\rightleftharpoons$ H$^+$+e$^-$ toward ions, removing the absorbers. The product of the two effects peaks near 10,000 K; hotter O and B stars have ionised hydrogen, cooler stars have almost no $n=2$ atoms.

s2-l006-saha-ionization-hr-diagram.prompt: Two stars have the same temperature, but one is a low-density giant atmosphere and the other a high-density dwarf atmosphere. In which is hydrogen (or any element) more highly ionized, and why?
options: The giant: lower density means a lower electron density, and Saha shifts the equilibrium toward ions.
The dwarf: higher density means more frequent collisions, and these ionize more atoms.
Both equally, since the Saha equation depends only on temperature and ionization energy.
The dwarf: at higher density the gas is hotter, and a hotter gas is more ionized.
s2-l006-saha-ionization-hr-diagram.explanation: Saha: $n_{i+1}n_e/n_i$ is fixed by $T$, so a smaller $n_e$ requires a larger ion fraction; it is Le Chatelier for $\mathrm{H}\rightleftharpoons\mathrm{H}^++e^-$. This is why spectral lines also reveal luminosity class.

s2-l006-saha-ionization-hr-diagram.prompt: A star has luminosity $L=100\,L_\odot$ and effective temperature 5000 K. Use $R/R_\odot=\sqrt{L/L_\odot}\,(5772\ {\rm K}/T)^2$ to compute its radius in solar radii.
s2-l006-saha-ionization-hr-diagram.explanation: $R/R_\odot=10\times(5772/5000)^2=13.3$: a cool, luminous G/K giant sits above the main sequence on the HR diagram.

s2-l007-hydrostatic-equilibrium-central-.prompt: In a star in hydrostatic equilibrium, how must pressure vary with radius, and why?
options: Pressure must be uniform, otherwise the star would drive winds.
Pressure must increase outward to push the gas away from the centre.
Pressure matters only at the centre; the outer layers float freely.
Pressure must increase inward ($dP/dr<0$).
s2-l007-hydrostatic-equilibrium-central-.explanation: For a shell of thickness $dr$, $dP\,dA=-g\rho\,dr\,dA$ with $g=GM_r/r^2$: the pressure difference across the shell balances its weight.

s2-l007-hydrostatic-equilibrium-central-.prompt: Two stars have the same radius, but star B has twice the mass of star A. By hydrostatic equilibrium, roughly how do their central pressures compare ($P_c\sim GM^2/R^4$)?
options: Star B has about twice the central pressure.
Both have the same central pressure, since the radius is the same.
Star B has about half the central pressure, since it is more tightly bound.
Star B has about four times the central pressure.
s2-l007-hydrostatic-equilibrium-central-.explanation: The weight of the overlying layers scales as $M\cdot M/R^2$ over an area $\sim R^2$, giving $P_c\sim GM^2/R^4$: doubling the mass quadruples the pressure needed to hold the star up.

s2-l007-hydrostatic-equilibrium-central-.prompt: Estimate the Sun's central pressure from the scaling $P_c\sim GM_\odot^2/R_\odot^4$, in units of $10^{15}$ Pa.
s2-l007-hydrostatic-equilibrium-central-.explanation: $P_c\sim(6.67\times10^{-11})(1.99\times10^{30})^2/(6.96\times10^8)^4\approx1.1\times10^{15}$ Pa; the true central pressure ($2.5\times10^{16}$ Pa) is higher because the Sun is centrally condensed, but the scaling is right in order of magnitude.

s2-l007-hydrostatic-equilibrium-central-.prompt: Explain in your own words how balancing the weight of a thin spherical shell against the pressure difference across it leads to dP/dr = -G M_r rho / r^2, and what extra equation is needed to close the problem.
s2-l007-hydrostatic-equilibrium-central-.rubric: Full credit requires: shell of thickness dr has weight g rho dr per unit area with g = G M_r / r^2; the net pressure force per area is -dP; setting these equal gives the equation; M_r depends on the density profile so mass continuity dM_r/dr = 4 pi r^2 rho is needed.
s2-l007-hydrostatic-equilibrium-central-.modelAnswer: A thin shell of thickness $dr$ feels its weight per unit area, $g\rho\,dr$ with $g=GM_r/r^2$, pulling inward, and must be held up by the pressure difference $-dP$ across it. Balancing gives $dP/dr=-GM_r\rho/r^2$. Because $M_r$ depends on how the density is distributed, mass continuity $dM_r/dr=4\pi r^2\rho$ is needed to close the system.

s2-l008-virial-theorem-kelvin-helmholtz.prompt: By the virial theorem a gravitating gas star has negative heat capacity. What happens when such a star radiates energy away without any nuclear source?
options: It cools and expands, like an ordinary gas that loses energy to its surroundings.
It contracts, and half the released gravitational energy goes into heating the gas.
It cools and contracts, because losing energy always lowers the temperature.
Its temperature stays constant while the radius shrinks, like a gas condensing at a phase transition.
s2-l008-virial-theorem-kelvin-helmholtz.explanation: $2K+U=0$ gives $E=K+U=-K$: losing energy $\Delta E<0$ means $K$ (temperature) increases. This negative heat capacity drives protostars to ignite their cores.

s2-l008-virial-theorem-kelvin-helmholtz.prompt: Estimate the Kelvin-Helmholtz timescale of the Sun, $\tau_{KH}\sim GM_\odot^2/(R_\odot L_\odot)$, in millions of years.
s2-l008-virial-theorem-kelvin-helmholtz.explanation: $GM_\odot^2/R_\odot=3.8\times10^{41}$ J, divided by $L_\odot=3.83\times10^{26}$ W gives $\approx10^{15}$ s $\approx30$ Myr, far shorter than the 4.6 Gyr age: gravity cannot power the Sun, so nuclear fusion must.

s2-l008-virial-theorem-kelvin-helmholtz.prompt: Explain physically why a contracting star heats up even though it is radiating energy away, using the virial theorem.
s2-l008-virial-theorem-kelvin-helmholtz.rubric: Full credit requires: virial theorem 2K + U = 0 so E = K + U = -K = U/2; contraction lowers U (more negative); half of the released energy radiated, half goes into K (thermal energy), so T rises; total energy decreases while temperature rises: negative heat capacity.
s2-l008-virial-theorem-kelvin-helmholtz.modelAnswer: For a self-gravitating gas $2K+U=0$, so the total energy is $E=K+U=-K$. When the star radiates, $E$ becomes more negative, which means $K$ (thermal energy) must increase: the star contracts, and half of the gravitational energy released goes into heating while the other half is radiated. Self-gravitating systems have negative heat capacity.

s2-l009-gas-radiation-pressure.prompt: Which star is more likely to have its interior pressure dominated by radiation rather than gas, and why?
options: A 50 $M_\odot$ star: higher interior temperature and lower density, so $P_{\rm rad}\propto T^4$ outgrows $P_{\rm gas}\propto\rho T$.
A 0.5 $M_\odot$ star, because it has less gas pressure and its cooler interior contains fewer particles to resist the photons, so the photons win out.
Both equally, since photons are present in every star and exert the same pressure.
A white dwarf, since it is the hottest of all stellar objects and the photons carry the most pressure.
s2-l009-gas-radiation-pressure.explanation: $P_{\rm rad}/P_{\rm gas}\propto T^3/\rho$ rises steeply with mass; radiation pressure also limits the maximum mass of stars.

s2-l009-gas-radiation-pressure.prompt: A fully ionised mixture has mass fractions $X=0.70$ (hydrogen), $Y=0.28$ (helium) and $Z=0.02$ (metals). Using $\mu^{-1}\approx2X+\tfrac34Y+\tfrac12Z$, compute the mean molecular weight $\mu$.
s2-l009-gas-radiation-pressure.explanation: $\mu^{-1}=2(0.70)+0.75(0.28)+0.5(0.02)=1.62$, so $\mu=0.617$. Ionised hydrogen gives two particles per proton mass, hence $\mu=1/2$.

s2-l009-gas-radiation-pressure.prompt: Near the Sun's centre, $\rho=1.5\times10^5$ kg/m$^3$, $T=1.57\times10^7$ K and $\mu=0.62$. Compute the ratio $P_{\rm rad}/P_{\rm gas}$, with $P_{\rm gas}=\rho kT/(\mu m_H)$, $P_{\rm rad}=aT^4/3$ and $a=7.566\times10^{-16}$ J m$^{-3}$K$^{-4}$. Give the answer in units of $10^{-4}$.
s2-l009-gas-radiation-pressure.explanation: $P_{\rm gas}=3.1\times10^{16}$ Pa and $P_{\rm rad}=1.5\times10^{13}$ Pa, so the ratio is $4.9\times10^{-4}$: gas pressure dominates in the Sun, radiation pressure is negligible.

s2-l009-gas-radiation-pressure.prompt: Explain why a fully ionized hydrogen gas has a mean molecular weight of 1/2, and why ionization matters for the pressure a star can provide.
s2-l009-gas-radiation-pressure.rubric: Full credit requires: each hydrogen atom gives one proton plus one electron, i.e. two free particles per proton mass; pressure depends on the number of particles (P = n k T), so mu = m_avg/m_H = 1/2; neutral hydrogen would have mu = 1 and give half the pressure at the same density and temperature.
s2-l009-gas-radiation-pressure.modelAnswer: In fully ionized hydrogen each atom of mass $m_H$ supplies two free particles, a proton and an electron, so the mean mass per particle is $m_H/2$ and $\mu=1/2$. Since $P=nkT$ counts particles, ionized gas exerts twice the pressure of neutral gas at the same density and temperature, which is part of why the hot interior of a star can support itself.

s2-l010-electron-degeneracy-pressure.prompt: A white dwarf has cooled to nearly zero temperature but still resists gravity. What provides the pressure?
options: Thermal pressure from residual heat, since the interior is still hot enough to resist gravity for billions of years of cooling.
Radiation pressure from trapped photons, which are confined by the star's high opacity.
Electron degeneracy pressure: squeezed electrons are forced into high-momentum states (Pauli), independent of temperature.
Nuclear fusion in the core, which continues at a slow rate after the star has cooled.
s2-l010-electron-degeneracy-pressure.explanation: Confining electrons to spacing $\Delta x\sim n^{-1/3}$ requires $p\gtrsim\hbar/\Delta x$ (uncertainty), and the exclusion principle stacks them in momentum space. The result $P\propto\rho^{5/3}$ is the free-electron gas of a metal.

s2-l010-electron-degeneracy-pressure.prompt: For nonrelativistic degenerate electrons $P\propto\rho^{5/3}$, but for ultrarelativistic ones $P\propto\rho^{4/3}$. What is the physical reason for the softer scaling?
options: Relativistic electrons obey Bose statistics, which allows more of them to occupy the lowest state.
Electron speed approaches $c$ and stops growing with momentum, so extra compression yields less extra pressure.
Relativistic electrons are no longer confined, so their wavefunctions spread out and relieve the pressure.
The Pauli principle weakens at high density, so electrons can pile into fewer momentum states.
s2-l010-electron-degeneracy-pressure.explanation: Pressure is momentum flux $\sim n p v$. Non-relativistically $v\propto p$, but as $v\to c$ it saturates, so $P\propto n\,p_F\,c\propto\rho^{4/3}$ instead of $\rho^{5/3}$.

s2-l010-electron-degeneracy-pressure.prompt: A carbon white-dwarf interior has $\rho=10^9$ kg/m$^3$, $T=10^7$ K, $\mu=1.7$ for the ions plus electrons and $\mu_e=2$. Compute the ratio $P_{\rm deg}/P_{\rm gas}$ with $P_{\rm gas}=\rho kT/\mu m_H$ and $P_{\rm deg}=\frac{(3\pi^2)^{2/3}\hbar^2}{5m_e}\left(\frac{\rho}{\mu_em_H}\right)^{5/3}$.
s2-l010-electron-degeneracy-pressure.explanation: $P_{\rm deg}\approx3.1\times10^{21}$ Pa and $P_{\rm gas}\approx4.9\times10^{19}$ Pa, a ratio near 64: degeneracy pressure dominates and is independent of $T$, so the star can cool without collapsing.

s2-l010-electron-degeneracy-pressure.prompt: Explain, using the Pauli principle and the uncertainty principle, why compressing electrons raises their pressure even at zero temperature.
s2-l010-electron-degeneracy-pressure.rubric: Full credit requires: electrons confined to small volume have large momentum uncertainty (p ~ hbar / spacing); Pauli exclusion prevents all from occupying the lowest state, so they fill states up to Fermi momentum p_F ~ hbar n^(1/3); the resulting kinetic energy/momentum flux is pressure independent of temperature; denser means larger p_F and higher pressure.
s2-l010-electron-degeneracy-pressure.modelAnswer: Compressing electrons to a number density $n$ confines each to a region of size $\sim n^{-1/3}$, so the uncertainty principle requires a momentum $\sim\hbar n^{1/3}$. The Pauli principle forbids them all from sharing the lowest state, so they fill momentum states up to a Fermi momentum $p_F\sim\hbar n^{1/3}$. These fast electrons carry momentum flux, i.e. pressure, with no dependence on temperature, and the pressure rises as the density rises.

s2-l011-mass-defect-main-sequence-lifeti.prompt: Using atomic masses $m(^1{\rm H})=1.007825$ u and $m(^4{\rm He})=4.002603$ u, compute the energy released in $4\,^1{\rm H}\to{}^4{\rm He}$ (ignore the neutrinos' share) in MeV (1 u $=931.494$ MeV$/c^2$).
Fusing hydrogen to helium converts about 0.7% of the rest mass to energy, whereas burning a hydrocarbon converts only about $10^{-10}$ of it. Why the huge difference?
options: Fusion happens at much higher temperature, and heat alone converts more mass into energy.
Nuclear binding energies are MeV per nucleon, millions of times the eV scale of chemical bonds.
Chemical reactions rearrange atoms, which cannot change mass at all, while fusion does.
Nuclei contain more particles than molecules do, so every fusion event releases more bonds.
s2-l011-mass-defect-main-sequence-lifeti.explanation: Energy released per reaction is set by the binding-energy change: roughly 1 eV for chemical bonds versus roughly 1-8 MeV per nucleon for nuclear binding. The mass defect in chemistry exists but is far below $10^{-9}$ of the mass.

s2-l011-mass-defect-main-sequence-lifeti.prompt: Assume 10% of the Sun's mass is available as fuel and 0.7% of that mass is converted to energy at the present luminosity. Estimate the main-sequence lifetime $t=0.1M_\odot(0.007)c^2/L_\odot$ in billions of years.
Explain why more massive stars live much shorter lives on the main sequence despite having more fuel.
s2-l011-mass-defect-main-sequence-lifeti.rubric: Full credit requires: fuel supply is proportional to mass M, but luminosity rises much faster (roughly M^3 to M^3.5) so lifetime t ~ M/L ~ M^-2 to M^-2.5; massive stars have higher central T and density, fusion rate rises steeply; they exhaust fuel faster.
s2-l011-mass-defect-main-sequence-lifeti.modelAnswer: Fuel available scales as $M$, but luminosity scales roughly as $M^3$ or $M^{3.5}$ because a larger mass compresses the core hotter, and fusion rates rise steeply with temperature. The lifetime $t\sim M/L$ therefore falls as roughly $M^{-2}$ to $M^{-2.5}$: a 10 $M_\odot$ star burns out in tens of millions of years, while a 0.5 $M_\odot$ star lasts longer than the age of the universe.

s2-l012-tunneling-gamow-peak-pp-cno.prompt: How does the Sun fuse hydrogen at a core temperature of $1.5\times10^7$ K when the Coulomb barrier between protons is of order MeV, far above $kT\approx1$ keV?
options: Protons at the Sun's centre are accelerated to MeV energies by magnetic fields in the core.
The Coulomb repulsion is screened to zero by the surrounding electrons, so there is effectively no barrier to overcome.
Quantum tunnelling through the barrier, combined with the Boltzmann tail of the thermal distribution.
The core temperature is actually $10^{10}$ K, and the quoted value is only the surface temperature.
s2-l012-tunneling-gamow-peak-pp-cno.explanation: The Boltzmann factor $e^{-E/kT}$ falls with $E$ while the tunnelling probability $e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$ rises; their product peaks sharply at $E\sim5$-10 keV. It is analogous to an Arrhenius rate with a barrier.

s2-l012-tunneling-gamow-peak-pp-cno.prompt: The pp chain's rate scales roughly as $T^4$ and the CNO cycle's as $T^{16}$-$T^{20}$. What follows?
options: The pp chain dominates in stars like the Sun.
CNO dominates in the Sun because it releases more energy per reaction.
The pp chain dominates in massive stars since CNO requires carbon-free gas.
They contribute equally at all stellar masses.
s2-l012-tunneling-gamow-peak-pp-cno.explanation: Below about $1.7\times10^7$ K pp wins; above, the steeper CNO rate wins. The steepness makes energy generation concentrated at the centre, favouring convection.

s2-l012-tunneling-gamow-peak-pp-cno.prompt: Two protons at separation 1.4 fm face a Coulomb barrier $e^2/4\pi\epsilon_0r$ (use $e^2/4\pi\epsilon_0=1.44$ MeV fm). At $T=1.57\times10^7$ K, how many times larger than $kT$ is this barrier?
s2-l012-tunneling-gamow-peak-pp-cno.explanation: The barrier is $1.44/1.4=1.03$ MeV, while $kT=1.35$ keV, a ratio of about 760. Essentially no protons reach the top thermally, so the rate is set by tunnelling from the Boltzmann tail.

s2-l012-tunneling-gamow-peak-pp-cno.prompt: Explain why the fusion rate in a star peaks at an intermediate energy (the Gamow peak) rather than at the highest or lowest energies available, and how this resembles an Arrhenius rate.
s2-l012-tunneling-gamow-peak-pp-cno.rubric: Full credit requires: Boltzmann factor e^(-E/kT) falls with energy (few particles at high E); tunnelling probability e^(-sqrt(E_G/E)) rises with energy; the product is sharply peaked at a few keV; in Arrhenius kinetics the rate also combines a thermal Boltzmann tail with a barrier, and rises steeply with T.
s2-l012-tunneling-gamow-peak-pp-cno.modelAnswer: The number of protons falls off as the Boltzmann factor $e^{-E/kT}$, while the probability of tunnelling through the Coulomb barrier rises with energy as $e^{-\sqrt{E_G/E}}$. Their product is a narrow peak (the Gamow peak) at a few keV, far above $kT$ but far below the barrier top. Like an Arrhenius rate, it combines a thermal tail with a barrier factor and so is extremely sensitive to temperature.

s2-l013-energy-transport-structure-equat.prompt: In the Sun, energy is carried by radiation in the inner region but by convection in the outer ~30% by radius. Why does convection take over there?
options: Because the outer region is hotter than the core.
Because there are no photons in the outer layers.
Because convection is always more efficient than radiation, so it operates wherever it is allowed.
Near the surface the gas is cooler and more opaque.
s2-l013-energy-transport-structure-equat.explanation: The radiative gradient $dT/dr\propto\kappa\rho L/T^3r^2$ grows with opacity and falls with temperature. Convection occurs where it would exceed the adiabatic gradient, e.g. in cool envelopes or in cores with very steep energy generation.

s2-l013-energy-transport-structure-equat.prompt: In the radiative-gradient equation $dT/dr=-3\kappa\rho L_r/(64\pi\sigma r^2T^3)$, what happens to the temperature gradient if the opacity $\kappa$ of a layer doubles and everything else stays fixed?
options: It halves, because opaque gas holds the heat in and the layer stays almost isothermal.
It is unchanged, because the gradient depends only on the luminosity passing through.
It steepens fourfold, because photon scattering grows as the square of the opacity.
It doubles in steepness: opaque gas needs a steeper gradient to carry the same flux, making convection more likely.
s2-l013-energy-transport-structure-equat.explanation: For a fixed luminosity, photons diffuse more slowly through opaque gas, so a steeper $T$ gradient is needed to drive the flux. Once the gradient exceeds the adiabatic one, convection takes over (cool, opaque envelopes).

s2-l013-energy-transport-structure-equat.prompt: In your own words, say what physical statement each of the four equations of stellar structure makes, and what boundary conditions pin down a solution.
s2-l013-energy-transport-structure-equat.rubric: Full credit requires: mass continuity (mass of shell = density times volume); hydrostatic equilibrium (pressure gradient balances gravity); energy generation (luminosity added by fusion in each shell); energy transport (temperature gradient needed to carry the flux, radiative or convective); boundary conditions M_r = L_r = 0 at centre and P, T -> 0 at surface.
s2-l013-energy-transport-structure-equat.modelAnswer: Mass continuity relates the mass in a shell to the density; hydrostatic equilibrium balances the pressure gradient against gravity; the energy-generation equation says the luminosity grows through a shell by the fusion power released there; the transport equation gives the temperature gradient needed to carry that flux by radiation or convection. They are closed with $M_r=L_r=0$ at the centre and $P,T\to0$ at the surface.

s2-l014-homology-mass-luminosity-stellar.prompt: The Vogt-Russell theorem says that the mass and chemical composition of a star determine its structure. What makes this plausible?
options: Stars with the same mass always have the same radius by definition, whatever their age or composition.
The four structure equations (mass, hydrostatic equilibrium, energy generation, transport) with boundary conditions form a closed system with a unique solution.
The theorem says rotation and magnetic fields never matter, whatever the star's history, so any two stars of equal mass and age are physically identical twins.
It says all stars of the same colour have the same mass, which follows from the main sequence.
s2-l014-homology-mass-luminosity-stellar.explanation: Four first-order ODEs for $M_r,P,L_r,T$ with conditions at the centre ($M_r=L_r=0$) and surface ($P,T\to0$) fix a unique structure; numerical shooting integrates from both ends and matches.

s2-l014-homology-mass-luminosity-stellar.prompt: Homology and the radiative diffusion equation give $L\propto M^3$ roughly for main-sequence stars. What does this imply for lifetimes?
options: Lifetime $t\propto M^3$: more massive stars live longer.
Lifetime $t\propto M/L\propto M^{-2}$.
Lifetime is independent of mass.
Lifetime $t\propto M^{-3}$ exactly, from the luminosity alone.
s2-l014-homology-mass-luminosity-stellar.explanation: Fuel $\propto M$, burn rate $\propto L\propto M^3$, so $t\propto M^{-2}$ (about $M^{-2.5}$ with the observed $L\propto M^{3.5}$).

s2-l014-homology-mass-luminosity-stellar.prompt: Take $t_{\rm MS}=10\ {\rm Gyr}\times(M/M_\odot)/(L/L_\odot)$ and $L\propto M^3$. Compute the main-sequence lifetime of a $5\,M_\odot$ star in Myr.
Describe in your own words how a numerical stellar model is built by 'shooting' from the centre and the surface, and what condition must be satisfied for a real star.
s2-l014-homology-mass-luminosity-stellar.rubric: Full credit requires: integrate the four ODEs outward from the centre with trial central P, T and inward from the surface with boundary conditions; the solutions must match at a fitting point (continuity of M, P, L, T); adjusting trial parameters until they do; for given mass and composition this gives a unique structure.
s2-l014-homology-mass-luminosity-stellar.modelAnswer: Guess central values of $P$ and $T$ and integrate the four equations outward (with $M_r=L_r=0$ at the centre); separately integrate inward from the surface using $P,T\to0$. The two solutions must agree at a fitting point; the guessed parameters are adjusted until $M_r$, $L_r$, $P$ and $T$ all match. By Vogt-Russell, one solution exists for a given mass and composition.

s2-l015-jeans-collapse-protostars.prompt: According to the Jeans criterion, which gas clouds are most prone to collapse and form stars?
options: Hot, tenuous clouds, because high thermal energy pulls the gas together and makes it collapse.
Cold, tenuous clouds, because they have lower pressure and so little to resist gravity.
Only clouds that are already rotating, since rotation supplies the angular momentum needed.
Cold, dense clouds: the Jeans mass $\propto T^{3/2}\rho^{-1/2}$ is small.
s2-l015-jeans-collapse-protostars.explanation: Collapse needs gravity (binding energy $\sim GM^2/R$) to beat thermal pressure ($\sim MkT/\mu m_H$). Lower $T$ and higher $\rho$ lower the mass threshold.

s2-l015-jeans-collapse-protostars.prompt: Why do newly forming protostars descend nearly vertically on the HR diagram along the Hayashi track?
options: They are fully convective with a cool surface fixed near $4000$ K.
They are cooling rapidly, so their temperature falls while luminosity is constant.
They are rapidly heating while the radius stays constant.
They are fusing hydrogen on the main sequence.
s2-l015-jeans-collapse-protostars.explanation: A fully convective star has a minimum surface temperature (the Hayashi limit), so contraction at fixed $T_{\rm eff}$ lowers $L=4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$ vertically.

s2-l015-jeans-collapse-protostars.prompt: Estimate the Jeans mass of a dense cloud core with $T=10$ K, $\mu=2.3$ and $\rho_0=10^{-17}$ kg/m$^3$, using $M_J\approx\left(\frac{5kT}{G\mu m_H}\right)^{3/2}\left(\frac{3}{4\pi\rho_0}\right)^{1/2}$. Give the answer in solar masses.
s2-l015-jeans-collapse-protostars.explanation: $\left(5kT/G\mu m_H\right)^{3/2}=1.39\times10^{23}$ and $\left(3/4\pi\rho_0\right)^{1/2}=1.55\times10^{8}$, so $M_J=2.2\times10^{31}$ kg $\approx11\,M_\odot$, the typical mass scale of fragmenting cloud cores.

s2-l015-jeans-collapse-protostars.prompt: Explain physically why a cloud of gas collapses when its mass exceeds the Jeans mass, by comparing gravity with thermal pressure.
s2-l015-jeans-collapse-protostars.rubric: Full credit requires: gravitational binding energy ~ G M^2 / R grows as M^2 while thermal energy ~ M k T / (mu m_H) grows as M; for large enough M gravity wins (virial theorem violated); lower T and higher density reduce the Jeans mass, so cold dense clouds fragment and collapse.
s2-l015-jeans-collapse-protostars.modelAnswer: The gravitational energy of a cloud scales like $GM^2/R$ while its thermal energy scales like $MkT/\mu m_H$. Gravity grows faster with mass, so beyond the Jeans mass thermal pressure cannot hold the cloud up (the virial condition fails) and it collapses. Cold, dense clouds have the smallest Jeans masses and are the ones that form stars.

s2-l016-post-main-sequence-evolution-clu.prompt: Compare the end of a 1 $M_\odot$ star with that of a 10 $M_\odot$ star.
options: Both become white dwarfs, but the 10 $M_\odot$ star does so faster.
The 1 $M_\odot$ star explodes as a supernova and the 10 $M_\odot$ star becomes a white dwarf instead.
The 1 $M_\odot$ star ends as a white dwarf; the 10 $M_\odot$ star dies in a core-collapse supernova.
Both end as black holes, the more massive one forming a larger hole.
s2-l016-post-main-sequence-evolution-clu.explanation: The core of the Sun-like star never gets hot enough to burn carbon; electron degeneracy halts its collapse. A massive star's core passes the Chandrasekhar limit and collapses.

s2-l016-post-main-sequence-evolution-clu.prompt: When hydrogen is exhausted in a star's core, the star becomes a red giant. What happens inside?
options: The inert core contracts and heats while a hydrogen-burning shell drives the envelope outward.
The whole star contracts, heats up and shifts bluer, since fusion has stopped to hold it up.
Fusion moves outward and the core cools and expands, which makes the surface cooler and redder.
The star radiates away its envelope, leaving a bare core at the same size as before.
s2-l016-post-main-sequence-evolution-clu.explanation: With no core fusion the helium core contracts (virial heating) until a surrounding hydrogen shell ignites; the extra luminosity inflates the envelope, which cools to red. Eventually the core gets hot enough to ignite helium.

s2-l016-post-main-sequence-evolution-clu.prompt: A cluster's main-sequence turnoff is at $2\,M_\odot$. Using $t_{\rm MS}\approx10\ {\rm Gyr}\,(M/M_\odot)^{-2.5}$, estimate the cluster age in Gyr.
s2-l016-post-main-sequence-evolution-clu.explanation: $t=10\times2^{-2.5}=1.77$ Gyr. Stars above $2\,M_\odot$ have already left the main sequence, so the cluster is about this old.

s2-l016-post-main-sequence-evolution-clu.prompt: Explain how the main-sequence turnoff of a star cluster tells you the cluster's age.
s2-l016-post-main-sequence-evolution-clu.rubric: Full credit requires: stars in a cluster formed together; more massive stars have shorter main-sequence lifetimes (t ~ M^-2.5) so leave the MS first; the most massive stars still on the MS mark the turnoff; their lifetime equals the cluster age; a lower (redder) turnoff means an older cluster.
s2-l016-post-main-sequence-evolution-clu.modelAnswer: All stars in a cluster formed at about the same time. The more massive ones exhaust hydrogen first, so the main sequence is 'peeled off' from the top. The luminosity (mass) of the stars at the turnoff gives their main-sequence lifetime, which must equal the cluster's age; a redder, fainter turnoff means an older cluster.

s2-l017-white-dwarf-structure-mass-radiu.prompt: A white dwarf accretes mass from a companion. How does its radius change, and why is this counterintuitive?
options: It grows ($R\propto M^{1/3}$) like a planet.
It stays constant because degeneracy pressure does not depend on density.
It grows because the gas heats up.
It shrinks ($R\propto M^{-1/3}$): more mass means more gravity.
s2-l017-white-dwarf-structure-mass-radiu.explanation: Balancing $P_c\sim GM^2/R^4$ against $P\propto(M/R^3)^{5/3}$ gives $R\propto M^{-1/3}$: the more massive a white dwarf, the smaller it is.

s2-l017-white-dwarf-structure-mass-radiu.prompt: A white dwarf has mass $0.6\,M_\odot$ and radius $8.7\times10^6$ m (about 1.4 Earth radii). Compute its mean density in kg/m$^3$, in units of $10^8$.
s2-l017-white-dwarf-structure-mass-radiu.explanation: $\rho=M/(\tfrac43\pi R^3)=1.19\times10^{30}/(2.76\times10^{21})=4.3\times10^{8}$ kg/m$^3$: a teaspoon would weigh several tonnes.

s2-l017-white-dwarf-structure-mass-radiu.prompt: Show how balancing gravity against nonrelativistic electron degeneracy pressure gives the white-dwarf mass-radius relation $R\propto M^{-1/3}$.
s2-l017-white-dwarf-structure-mass-radiu.rubric: Full credit requires: gravity needs central pressure P ~ G M^2 / R^4; degenerate NR pressure P ~ (M/R^3)^(5/3) = M^(5/3) R^(-5); equating gives R proportional to M^(-1/3); heavier white dwarfs are smaller.
s2-l017-white-dwarf-structure-mass-radiu.modelAnswer: Hydrostatic equilibrium needs a central pressure $P\sim GM^2/R^4$. Nonrelativistic degeneracy pressure is $P\propto\rho^{5/3}\sim(M/R^3)^{5/3}=M^{5/3}R^{-5}$. Setting them equal gives $R\propto M^{-1/3}$: adding mass squeezes the star smaller.

s2-l018-chandrasekhar-limit-type-ia.prompt: Why do Type Ia supernovae serve as good standard candles?
options: They come from massive stars, which all have identical masses and therefore explode with identical energy each time.
They result from white dwarfs reaching nearly the same mass (the Chandrasekhar limit) and igniting.
They always occur in the same galaxy, so the distance to every one of them is the same.
Their light is polarised in a standard way that reveals the intrinsic brightness.
s2-l018-chandrasekhar-limit-type-ia.explanation: Reaching about $1.4\,M_\odot$ triggers runaway carbon fusion, leaving a repeatable explosion (after correcting for light-curve width).

s2-l018-chandrasekhar-limit-type-ia.prompt: A white dwarf has no nuclear fusion. What powers the light it radiates as it ages?
options: Slow gravitational contraction, which converts potential energy to heat as the star shrinks.
Residual hydrogen burning in a thin outer shell that continues for billions of years.
Stored thermal energy of its ions, released slowly through a thin insulating envelope as the star cools.
Radioactive decay of the heavy elements formed in its core, which keeps it warm.
s2-l018-chandrasekhar-limit-type-ia.explanation: Degeneracy pressure does not depend on temperature, so the star cannot contract as it cools; it just radiates its ion thermal energy, dimming over billions of years.

s2-l018-chandrasekhar-limit-type-ia.prompt: Using $M_{\rm Ch}\simeq5.83\,M_\odot/\mu_e^2$, compute the Chandrasekhar mass, in solar masses, for an iron core of $^{56}$Fe ($\mu_e=56/26$).
s2-l018-chandrasekhar-limit-type-ia.explanation: $\mu_e=2.154$, so $M_{\rm Ch}=5.83/4.64=1.26\,M_\odot$, smaller than the 1.46 $M_\odot$ for carbon/oxygen ($\mu_e=2$).

s2-l018-chandrasekhar-limit-type-ia.prompt: Explain in your own words why electron degeneracy pressure cannot support a white dwarf above a maximum mass.
s2-l018-chandrasekhar-limit-type-ia.rubric: Full credit requires: at higher mass the density rises and electrons become relativistic; degeneracy pressure softens from rho^(5/3) to rho^(4/3), which scales with density the same as gravity needs; beyond the limit gravity wins at all radii; mass about 1.4 solar masses; collapse follows.
s2-l018-chandrasekhar-limit-type-ia.modelAnswer: As mass increases, the star shrinks and the electrons are squeezed to relativistic momenta. Relativistic degeneracy pressure grows only as $\rho^{4/3}$ instead of $\rho^{5/3}$, which is just too soft to keep up with gravity. Above about $1.4\,M_\odot$ gravity wins at every radius and the star collapses.

s2-l019-core-collapse-supernovae.prompt: A supernova spectrum shows no hydrogen but strong silicon lines near maximum light. Which type is it, and what is its likely origin?
options: Type II, the core collapse of a massive star with hydrogen envelope.
Type Ic, the collapse of a star with its hydrogen and helium envelopes both stripped away.
Type Ia, the thermonuclear explosion of a white dwarf, not a core-collapse event.
Type II, the core collapse of a star in a binary system.
s2-l019-core-collapse-supernovae.explanation: Classification is by spectra: hydrogen lines mean Type II; no hydrogen with silicon means Ia; no hydrogen and little silicon (with or without helium) means Ib/c, which are core-collapse explosions of stripped massive stars.

s2-l019-core-collapse-supernovae.prompt: Why does fusion in a massive star stop building heavier elements at iron, leading to core collapse?
options: Iron nuclei are too heavy to tunnel through each other's Coulomb barrier at any temperature.
The star runs out of helium and carbon, and iron is the next element it happens to burn.
Iron has the highest binding energy per nucleon, so fusing or fissioning it no longer releases energy.
Iron is magnetic, so the core's field then suppresses any further nuclear reactions.
s2-l019-core-collapse-supernovae.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon peaks near $^{56}$Fe. Fusion up to iron releases energy and supports the star; beyond iron it absorbs energy, so the core has no more fuel and is left supported only by degeneracy pressure until it exceeds $M_{\rm Ch}$.

s2-l019-core-collapse-supernovae.prompt: Estimate the gravitational binding energy released when a $1.4\,M_\odot$ iron core collapses to a neutron star of radius 10 km, $E\sim GM^2/R$, in units of $10^{46}$ J.
s2-l019-core-collapse-supernovae.explanation: $E\approx(6.67\times10^{-11})(2.8\times10^{30})^2/10^4=5.2\times10^{46}$ J. A supernova's light and kinetic energy are only about $10^{44}$ J, i.e. $<1\%$; roughly 99% leaves as neutrinos.

s2-l019-core-collapse-supernovae.prompt: Explain why a core-collapse supernova releases roughly 99% of its energy as neutrinos rather than light or kinetic energy.
s2-l019-core-collapse-supernovae.rubric: Full credit requires: collapse of the iron core to a neutron star releases gravitational binding energy ~ G M^2 / R ~ 5e46 J; the dense, hot matter is opaque to photons but electron capture (neutronization) produces many neutrinos that escape; visible light and kinetic energy of ejecta are only ~1e44 J, under 1%.
s2-l019-core-collapse-supernovae.modelAnswer: Collapsing a $1.4\,M_\odot$ core to $\sim10$ km releases $GM^2/R\sim5\times10^{46}$ J. The core is so dense that photons are trapped, but neutrinos from electron capture (neutronization) and thermal pair processes stream out. The light and the kinetic energy of the ejecta amount to only $\sim10^{44}$ J, under 1% of the total.

s2-l020-neutron-stars-pulsars.prompt: Why is the neutron-star radius (about 10 km) so much smaller than a white dwarf's (about 6000 km) for similar mass?
options: Neutron degeneracy replaces electron degeneracy.
Neutron stars are held up by thermal pressure, which is larger.
Neutron stars are much heavier, so they pull themselves together.
Neutrons are lighter than electrons.
s2-l020-neutron-stars-pulsars.explanation: Degeneracy pressure at fixed density is $\propto1/m$, so heavier neutrons need a much higher density to support the same star: $\sim10^{17}$ kg/m$^3$, comparable to the nucleus.

s2-l020-neutron-stars-pulsars.prompt: Many neutron stars are known to exist, but only a fraction are observed as pulsars. Why?
options: The radio beam is narrow and sweeps past Earth only if its sweep happens to cross our line of sight.
Most neutron stars have no magnetic field, so they cannot produce radio emission.
Pulsations stop within a few years of the supernova, once the star has cooled down.
Only neutron stars in binary systems rotate fast enough to produce pulses we can see.
s2-l020-neutron-stars-pulsars.explanation: The lighthouse beam covers a small solid angle, and only observers inside it see pulses. Neutron stars whose beams miss Earth are invisible as pulsars.

s2-l020-neutron-stars-pulsars.prompt: The Crab pulsar has $P=0.0334$ s and $\dot P=4.2\times10^{-13}$. Using $B\approx3.2\times10^{19}\sqrt{P\dot P}$ G, compute its surface field in units of $10^{12}$ G.
s2-l020-neutron-stars-pulsars.explanation: $P\dot P=1.40\times10^{-14}$, so $B=3.2\times10^{19}\times1.18\times10^{-7}=3.8\times10^{12}$ G. The characteristic age $P/2\dot P\approx1260$ yr, close to the historical 1054 AD supernova.

s2-l020-neutron-stars-pulsars.prompt: Explain what a pulsar is and how its period $P$ and period derivative $\dot P$ allow estimates of its surface magnetic field and age.
s2-l020-neutron-stars-pulsars.rubric: Full credit requires: rotating magnetised neutron star whose magnetic axis is misaligned with spin axis, beams of radio emission sweep past Earth like a lighthouse; magnetic dipole radiation removes rotational energy so P increases slowly; B ~ 3.2e19 sqrt(P Pdot) gauss from dipole spin-down torque; characteristic age ~ P/(2 Pdot).
s2-l020-neutron-stars-pulsars.modelAnswer: A pulsar is a rapidly rotating, strongly magnetised neutron star whose radio beams, offset from the rotation axis, sweep over Earth once per rotation, like a lighthouse. The star slows as magnetic dipole radiation carries off rotational energy, so $P$ grows. The spin-down torque gives $B\sim3.2\times10^{19}\sqrt{P\dot P}$ G, and the age is roughly $P/(2\dot P)$.

s2-l021-black-holes-schwarzschild-radius.prompt: Compute the Schwarzschild radius $R_S=2GM/c^2$ of a $10\,M_\odot$ black hole, in kilometres.
s2-l021-black-holes-schwarzschild-radius.explanation: $R_S=2(6.67\times10^{-11})(1.99\times10^{31})/(3.00\times10^8)^2=2.95\times10^4$ m $\approx29.5$ km (about 3 km per solar mass).

s2-l021-black-holes-schwarzschild-radius.prompt: Suppose the Sun were suddenly replaced by a black hole of the same mass, $1\,M_\odot$. What would happen to Earth's orbit?
options: Earth would spiral inward, since a black hole sucks in all matter around it.
Earth would fly off, since without sunlight there would be no pressure to hold us.
Earth's orbit would shrink because gravity near a black hole is much stronger than near a star.
It would be unchanged: outside $r_s\approx3$ km the gravity is the same as for any mass $1\,M_\odot$.
s2-l021-black-holes-schwarzschild-radius.explanation: Newtonian-like gravity at large distance depends only on the enclosed mass. A black hole is dangerous only close to $r_s$; far away it gravitates like any other mass.

s2-l021-black-holes-schwarzschild-radius.prompt: A compact X-ray source orbiting a visible star is measured to have a mass of 8 solar masses. Explain why astronomers conclude it is a black hole rather than a neutron star.
s2-l021-black-holes-schwarzschild-radius.rubric: Full credit requires: degeneracy pressure of neutrons (like electrons) can support only up to a maximum mass, about 2-3 solar masses; a compact object well above that cannot be a neutron star or white dwarf, nor an ordinary star since it emits too little light; so it must be a black hole; mass from orbital dynamics of the companion.
s2-l021-black-holes-schwarzschild-radius.modelAnswer: Neutron degeneracy pressure can support a star only up to a maximum mass of roughly 2-3 solar masses, just as electron degeneracy has the Chandrasekhar limit. An 8 solar-mass object (measured from the visible star's orbit) that is also too dim to be a normal star has no known pressure that could hold it up, so it must have collapsed to a black hole.

s2-l022-milky-way-galaxy-types-enclosed-.prompt: The Milky Way's stellar halo contains old, metal-poor stars on randomly oriented orbits, while the disk contains younger, metal-richer stars on nearly circular orbits. What does this suggest?
options: The halo formed last, from heavy elements dumped by the disk during recent supernovae.
The halo formed early, from material that collapsed before enough heavy elements had been made.
Halo stars are old because they are far from the centre, where all the first stars formed.
Metal content has no link to formation history; it is set only by where a star now sits.
s2-l022-milky-way-galaxy-types-enclosed-.explanation: Metals are made by earlier generations of stars, so low-metallicity stars formed early. Their random orbits fit formation during a rapid, chaotic collapse, whereas the disk formed later, once gas had settled into rotation.

s2-l022-milky-way-galaxy-types-enclosed-.prompt: The Sun orbits the galactic centre at $v=220$ km/s at $r=8.0$ kpc. Compute the mass enclosed within the Sun's orbit, $M=v^2r/G$, in units of $10^{10}M_\odot$.
Explain how the Sun's orbital speed and distance from the Galactic centre let us estimate the mass of the Galaxy inside the Sun's orbit.
s2-l022-milky-way-galaxy-types-enclosed-.rubric: Full credit requires: circular orbit: gravitational force supplies centripetal force, G M m / r^2 = m v^2 / r; solve M = v^2 r / G; for a spherical distribution only the enclosed mass matters; plugging v ~ 220 km/s and r ~ 8 kpc gives ~1e11 solar masses.
s2-l022-milky-way-galaxy-types-enclosed-.modelAnswer: For a circular orbit gravity supplies the centripetal force, $GMm/r^2=mv^2/r$, so the mass enclosed within the orbit is $M(<r)=v^2r/G$ (for a roughly spherical distribution only the enclosed mass pulls). With $v\approx220$ km/s and $r\approx8$ kpc this gives about $10^{11}\,M_\odot$.

s2-l023-rotation-curves-dark-halos.prompt: Outside the visible disk of a spiral galaxy, we would expect orbital speeds to fall as $v\propto r^{-1/2}$ (Keplerian). Instead, rotation curves stay flat. What does this imply?
options: Gravity weakens more slowly than $1/r^2$ outside galaxies, for no further reason.
Stars at large radius are more massive, so they orbit faster.
The enclosed mass keeps growing roughly in proportion to $r$ ($M\propto v^2r/G$).
The visible stars must contain much more mass than we thought.
s2-l023-rotation-curves-dark-halos.explanation: For circular orbits $v^2=GM(<r)/r$. A flat $v$ means $M(<r)\propto r$. Gravitational lensing and cluster dynamics point to the same unseen mass.

s2-l023-rotation-curves-dark-halos.prompt: A galaxy has all its mass inside radius $r_0$. Compared with the orbital speed at $r_0$, what is the orbital speed of a star at $2r_0$?
options: It is the same, since the enclosed mass has not changed and gravity only depends on mass.
It is smaller by a factor of $\sqrt2$ (Keplerian), since the enclosed mass is the same but $r$ is doubled.
It is smaller by a factor of 2, since $v\propto1/r$ for a bound orbit.
It is larger by a factor of $\sqrt2$, since a star farther out must move faster to stay in orbit.
s2-l023-rotation-curves-dark-halos.explanation: $v=\sqrt{GM/r}$ with fixed $M$ gives $v\propto r^{-1/2}$. Observed curves do not fall like this, which is the signature of extra mass at large $r$.

s2-l023-rotation-curves-dark-halos.prompt: If the rotation speed stays flat at 220 km/s out to $r=50$ kpc, compute the enclosed mass there in units of $10^{11}M_\odot$.
s2-l023-rotation-curves-dark-halos.explanation: $M\propto r$: $9.0\times10^{10}\times50/8=5.6\times10^{11}\,M_\odot$, several times the visible mass (a few $10^{10}M_\odot$).

s2-l023-rotation-curves-dark-halos.prompt: Explain why flat rotation curves out to large radius imply the presence of dark matter, and what this says about how its mass is distributed.
s2-l023-rotation-curves-dark-halos.rubric: Full credit requires: v^2 = G M(<r) / r so constant v means M(<r) proportional to r; light falls off exponentially in the disk, so the extra mass is unseen; a halo with density proportional to 1/r^2 extending beyond the stars; mass in the halo several times the visible mass.
s2-l023-rotation-curves-dark-halos.modelAnswer: For circular orbits $v^2=GM(<r)/r$. If $v$ stays constant out to large $r$, then $M(<r)\propto r$ keeps growing even where the starlight has faded away. The extra mass is not luminous, so we infer an extended dark halo with density falling roughly as $1/r^2$, containing several times the visible mass.

s2-l024-distance-ladder-dark-matter-evid.prompt: Why do errors in the cosmic distance ladder compound as we go to larger distances?
options: Each rung (parallax, Cepheids, Type Ia supernovae) is calibrated using the one below it.
Because the speed of light changes at large distances, which distorts the flux measurements.
Because more distant objects are always fainter and so impossible to calibrate accurately by any method.
They don't; each rung is independent of the others and has its own calibration.
s2-l024-distance-ladder-dark-matter-evid.explanation: Parallax calibrates the Cepheid period-luminosity relation, which calibrates Type Ia supernova peak luminosity, which then measures distances to galaxies far into the Hubble flow.

s2-l024-distance-ladder-dark-matter-evid.prompt: A Type Ia supernova has peak absolute magnitude $M=-19.3$ and is observed at peak apparent magnitude $m=18.2$. Use the distance modulus to find its distance in Mpc.
s2-l024-distance-ladder-dark-matter-evid.explanation: $d=10^{(m-M+5)/5}$ pc $=10^{8.5}$ pc $=316$ Mpc. Any systematic error in the Cepheid calibration of $M$ propagates directly into this distance.

s2-l024-distance-ladder-dark-matter-evid.prompt: In the Bullet Cluster, two clusters have collided. The hot X-ray gas lags near the collision point, but gravitational lensing shows most of the mass lies ahead, with the galaxies. What does this show?
options: The hot gas carries most of the mass, and is slowed by the collision like the galaxies.
Gravity is stronger near the collision, so lensing overestimates the true mass there.
Dark matter collides strongly with itself and the gas, so it stays near the collision point.
Most of the mass is not the hot gas, and interacts only weakly, passing through the collision.
s2-l024-distance-ladder-dark-matter-evid.explanation: Gas (most of the visible baryons) is slowed by collisions; the lensing mass is offset from it and travels with the collisionless galaxies. So most of the mass is a separate, weakly interacting component.

s2-l024-distance-ladder-dark-matter-evid.prompt: List two independent lines of evidence for dark matter besides galaxy rotation curves and say what each shows.
s2-l024-distance-ladder-dark-matter-evid.rubric: Full credit requires two of: galaxy cluster dynamics (virial theorem velocities too high for visible mass); gravitational lensing (mass map from distortion exceeds visible); Bullet Cluster (lensing mass offset from hot X-ray gas, showing mass is collisionless and separate from baryons); CMB acoustic peaks / structure formation. Each with what it shows.
s2-l024-distance-ladder-dark-matter-evid.modelAnswer: Galaxy clusters: the galaxies' speeds are too high for the visible mass to bind them, implying several times more mass. Gravitational lensing: the bending of background light by clusters maps total mass, which far exceeds the luminous matter. The Bullet Cluster shows that after a collision the lensing mass lies with the galaxies, apart from the dominant hot gas, so the unseen mass is collisionless and separate from ordinary matter.

s2-l025-cosmological-principle-hubble-la.prompt: Distant galaxies recede from us with speed proportional to distance. Does this place the Milky Way at the centre of the universe?
options: Yes, because only the centre has everything receding.
Yes, but only at large scales.
No, because galaxies move randomly and the apparent recession pattern is just a coincidence.
No: in uniform expansion ($r=a(t)x$) every observer sees the same law, $v=Hr$.
s2-l025-cosmological-principle-hubble-la.explanation: For any two comoving points the separation grows as $a(t)$, so $v=\dot a x=(\dot a/a)r$ holds for any observer. Isotropy about every point implies homogeneity.

s2-l025-cosmological-principle-hubble-la.prompt: Estimate the Hubble time $1/H_0$ for $H_0=70$ km/s/Mpc, in billions of years (1 Mpc $=3.086\times10^{19}$ km, 1 yr $=3.156\times10^7$ s).
s2-l025-cosmological-principle-hubble-la.explanation: $1/H_0=3.086\times10^{19}/70=4.41\times10^{17}$ s $=14.0$ Gyr, close to the actual age of the universe.

s2-l025-cosmological-principle-hubble-la.prompt: A galaxy has redshift $z=0.020$. For small $z$, $d\approx cz/H_0$. Compute its distance for $H_0=70$ km/s/Mpc, in Mpc.
Starting from uniform expansion, in which every distance is $r=a(t)x$ with $x$ a fixed comoving coordinate, derive Hubble's law and say what $H$ is.
s2-l025-cosmological-principle-hubble-la.rubric: Full credit requires: differentiate r = a(t) x at fixed x: v = adot x = (adot/a) r; so v = H r with H = adot/a, the fractional expansion rate; applies to every observer; H depends on time and H0 is its present value.
s2-l025-cosmological-principle-hubble-la.modelAnswer: For galaxies at fixed comoving positions, $v=dr/dt=\dot a\,x=(\dot a/a)\,a x=Hr$, with $H=\dot a/a$ the fractional rate of change of the scale factor. The law holds for any observer, and $H_0$ is its present value.

s2-l026-scale-factor-redshift-robertson-.prompt: A distant galaxy is observed at redshift $z=1$. What does this tell us about the universe's size when the light was emitted?
options: The universe was twice its present size, since the wavelength doubled.
The universe was half its present size (the wavelength was stretched by $1+z=a_0/a_e=2$).
The galaxy was receding at the speed of light when it emitted the light, so the light was stretched.
The galaxy was exactly 1 Mpc away, since $z=1$ corresponds to 1 Mpc.
s2-l026-scale-factor-redshift-robertson-.explanation: Cosmological redshift is not an ordinary Doppler shift through space; it is the stretching of wavelengths by the scale factor, $1+z=a(t_0)/a(t_e)$.

s2-l026-scale-factor-redshift-robertson-.prompt: In the Robertson-Walker metric, two galaxies have fixed comoving separation $\chi$ (flat space, $k=0$). The scale factor doubles between two epochs. What happens to the proper distance between them?
options: It doubles, because proper distance is $a(t)\chi$ while the comoving separation stays fixed.
It stays the same, because comoving galaxies are not moving through space.
It halves, because the galaxies get closer together as the universe expands.
It increases by a factor of $\sqrt2$, because only half the expansion affects the separation.
s2-l026-scale-factor-redshift-robertson-.explanation: Proper distance is $d_p=a(t)\chi$. The galaxies do not move through space, but the space between them stretches in proportion to $a$.

s2-l026-scale-factor-redshift-robertson-.prompt: Light from a distant galaxy has a rest wavelength of 500 nm and is observed at 900 nm. Compute the scale factor $a(t_e)$ at emission, relative to $a(t_0)=1$.
s2-l026-scale-factor-redshift-robertson-.explanation: $1+z=\lambda_{\rm obs}/\lambda_{\rm em}=1.8$, so $a_e=1/(1+z)=0.556$: the universe was about 56% of its present size when the light left.

s2-l026-scale-factor-redshift-robertson-.prompt: Explain why cosmological redshift is described as the stretching of wavelengths by the expansion of space rather than as an ordinary Doppler shift, and what $1+z$ measures.
s2-l026-scale-factor-redshift-robertson-.rubric: Full credit requires: photon wavelength grows in proportion to the scale factor as it travels, lambda_obs / lambda_em = a(t0)/a(t_e) = 1 + z; the galaxy is at rest in comoving coordinates, so the shift is not caused by motion through space; z does not map simply to a velocity at large z.
s2-l026-scale-factor-redshift-robertson-.modelAnswer: A photon's wavelength grows in proportion to the scale factor while it travels, so $\lambda_{\rm obs}/\lambda_{\rm em}=a(t_0)/a(t_e)=1+z$. The galaxy is at rest in comoving coordinates; the shift comes from the space between us stretching, not from motion through space, so $1+z$ measures how much the universe has expanded since emission.

s2-l027-friedmann-fluid-acceleration-equ.prompt: Explain in your own words how the Newtonian argument for a test shell in an expanding sphere gives the Friedmann equation, and how the density relative to the critical density determines the fate.
s2-l027-friedmann-fluid-acceleration-equ.rubric: Full credit requires: energy conservation for a shell: kinetic energy (1/2) m rdot^2 minus gravitational potential -GMm/r = constant U; the sign of constant (curvature k): density > critical gives negative total energy (bound) so expansion turns around; < critical gives positive energy and unbound; equal gives marginal; equivalent to ball thrown from planet at escape speed.
s2-l027-friedmann-fluid-acceleration-equ.modelAnswer: A shell at radius $r$ in a uniform sphere obeys $\tfrac12\dot r^2-GM/r=U$ (constant), exactly like a ball thrown upward. Written with $r=a x$ and $M=\tfrac43\pi\rho r^3$, this is the Friedmann equation with the constant playing the role of curvature. If $\rho>\rho_c$ the total energy is negative (bound, would recollapse); if $\rho<\rho_c$ it is positive (expands forever); at $\rho=\rho_c$ it is exactly marginal (flat).

s2-l027-friedmann-fluid-acceleration-equ.prompt: The acceleration equation is $\ddot a/a=-(4\pi G/3c^2)(\varepsilon+3P)$. What is needed for the expansion to accelerate?
options: A large positive pressure, which pushes outward on the surrounding space and so accelerates it.
A large positive energy density alone, since gravity is attractive only for matter without pressure.
A pressure equal to one third of the energy density, as for radiation, which pushes harder than dust.
A negative pressure with $P<-\varepsilon/3$, such as a cosmological constant ($w=-1$).
s2-l027-friedmann-fluid-acceleration-equ.explanation: Ordinary matter and radiation have $\varepsilon+3P>0$ and decelerate the expansion. A cosmological constant has $P=-\varepsilon$, making $\varepsilon+3P=-2\varepsilon<0$.

s2-l027-friedmann-fluid-acceleration-equ.prompt: A comoving volume filled with photons expands adiabatically. Why does the photon energy inside it decrease, and where does the energy go?
options: The photons are absorbed by the matter, and the energy is stored as heat in the dust.
Energy is not conserved in an expanding universe, so the photon energy simply vanishes.
The photon gas does work $P\,dV$ on the expanding boundary, so its energy falls ($dE=-P\,dV$).
Photons leave the volume through its boundary, carrying the energy out into the empty space beyond.
s2-l027-friedmann-fluid-acceleration-equ.explanation: Applying the first law to a comoving volume $V\propto a^3$ gives $\dot\varepsilon+3(\dot a/a)(\varepsilon+P)=0$. For radiation $P=\varepsilon/3$, so $\varepsilon\propto a^{-4}$: the extra $1/a$ is the work done as wavelengths stretch.

s2-l028-equation-of-state-critical-densi.prompt: Why does the energy density of radiation fall faster with expansion ($\propto a^{-4}$) than that of non-relativistic matter ($\propto a^{-3}$)?
options: Because photons are destroyed by expansion, so their number density falls faster.
Both are diluted by the volume increase $a^3$, but photons also lose energy as their wavelengths stretch, giving an extra $1/a$.
Because radiation has no mass, it is not affected by gravity and so is diluted by more than the volume factor alone, whatever its energy.
Because matter is replenished from dark matter as space expands, while photons are not.
s2-l028-equation-of-state-critical-densi.explanation: The fluid equation gives $\rho\propto a^{-3(1+w)}$: $w=0$ for dust, $w=1/3$ for radiation, so $a^{-4}$.

s2-l028-equation-of-state-critical-densi.prompt: The density parameter $\Omega=\rho/\rho_c$ is measured to be greater than 1. What does that mean for the geometry?
options: Positive curvature (a closed universe, $k>0$).
Negative curvature (an open universe).
Flat geometry.
Nothing: $\Omega$ does not relate to geometry.
s2-l028-equation-of-state-critical-densi.explanation: The Friedmann equation gives $\Omega-1=kc^2/(H^2R_0^2a^2)$: sign of $k$ follows sign of $\Omega-1$.

s2-l028-equation-of-state-critical-densi.prompt: Compute the critical density $\rho_c=3H_0^2/(8\pi G)$ for $H_0=70$ km/s/Mpc in units of $10^{-27}$ kg/m$^3$.
s2-l028-equation-of-state-critical-densi.explanation: $H_0=2.27\times10^{-18}$ s$^{-1}$, so $\rho_c=9.2\times10^{-27}$ kg/m$^3$, about 5.5 hydrogen atoms per cubic metre.

s2-l028-equation-of-state-critical-densi.prompt: Explain in your own words why a cosmological constant (w = -1) has a density that stays constant as the universe expands, while matter and radiation are diluted.
s2-l028-equation-of-state-critical-densi.rubric: Full credit requires: fluid equation gives rho proportional to a^(-3(1+w)); for w = -1 the exponent is zero; negative pressure P = -epsilon does work that exactly offsets the dilution from volume growth; so energy per volume is constant, like vacuum energy.
s2-l028-equation-of-state-critical-densi.modelAnswer: The fluid equation gives $\rho\propto a^{-3(1+w)}$. For $w=-1$ the exponent vanishes. A fluid with pressure $P=-\varepsilon$ gains energy as its volume grows (the work $-P\,dV$ is positive), exactly offsetting the dilution, so its energy density is constant, as for vacuum energy.

s2-l029-single-component-universes-age.prompt: Which single-component flat universe has accelerating expansion, and why?
options: A matter-dominated universe, $a\propto t^{2/3}$, whose expansion speeds up with time.
A radiation-dominated universe, $a\propto t^{1/2}$, whose expansion speeds up with time.
A universe dominated by a cosmological constant, $a\propto e^{Ht}$.
All three accelerate; only the rate differs between them.
s2-l029-single-component-universes-age.explanation: For $a\propto t^{p}$ with $p<1$ the expansion decelerates ($\ddot a<0$). Only $w<-1/3$ gives acceleration.

s2-l029-single-component-universes-age.prompt: A flat matter-only universe with $H_0=70$ km/s/Mpc has age $2/(3H_0)\approx9.3$ Gyr, yet some stars are over 12 Gyr old. What does this suggest?
options: The stars' ages are wrong by definition.
The Hubble constant must be 0.
A matter-only universe is much older than 12 Gyr.
A matter-only universe is too young.
s2-l029-single-component-universes-age.explanation: With $\Omega_m\approx0.3$, $\Omega_\Lambda\approx0.7$ the integral for the age gives about 13.8 Gyr, consistent with old stars and with the CMB.

s2-l029-single-component-universes-age.prompt: Compute the age of a flat matter-only universe, $t_0=2/(3H_0)$, for $H_0=70$ km/s/Mpc, in Gyr.
Explain why a universe dominated by matter decelerates while one dominated by a cosmological constant accelerates, in terms of the power law $a\propto t^{p}$ and the sign of $\ddot a$.
s2-l029-single-component-universes-age.rubric: Full credit requires: a proportional to t^(2/(3(1+w))); matter p = 2/3 and radiation p = 1/2 are less than 1 so adot decreases with time (decelerating); Lambda gives exponential growth with ddot a > 0; the sign is set by epsilon + 3P (w > -1/3 decelerates, w < -1/3 accelerates).
s2-l029-single-component-universes-age.modelAnswer: For $a\propto t^{p}$ the acceleration is $\ddot a\propto p(p-1)t^{p-2}$, negative when $p<1$. Matter ($p=2/3$) and radiation ($p=1/2$) therefore decelerate, because their $\varepsilon+3P>0$ makes gravity attractive. A cosmological constant has $P=-\varepsilon$, so $\varepsilon+3P<0$ and gravity effectively repels, giving exponential growth $e^{Ht}$ with $\ddot a>0$.

s2-l030-benchmark-model-equality-fate.prompt: Matter and radiation densities scale as $a^{-3}$ and $a^{-4}$. With $\Omega_m=0.31$ and $\Omega_r=9.2\times10^{-5}$ today, the two are equal at $a_{\rm eq}=\Omega_r/\Omega_m$. Compute $1+z_{\rm eq}=1/a_{\rm eq}$.
s2-l030-benchmark-model-equality-fate.explanation: $1+z_{\rm eq}=\Omega_m/\Omega_r=0.31/9.2\times10^{-5}=3.4\times10^{3}$, before recombination ($z\approx1100$): the early universe was radiation-dominated, then matter-dominated.

s2-l030-benchmark-model-equality-fate.prompt: In the benchmark model the universe is spatially flat with $\Omega_m\approx0.3$ and $\Omega_\Lambda\approx0.7$. What is its likely fate?
options: A Big Crunch, because a flat universe containing matter must eventually recollapse.
Expansion that slows to a halt but never reverses, because $\Omega_{\rm total}=1$ is exactly critical.
Eternal, accelerating expansion, because the cosmological constant dominates and does not dilute.
A Big Rip, because a flat universe with $\Omega_\Lambda>0$ must tear itself apart.
s2-l030-benchmark-model-equality-fate.explanation: Matter dilutes as $a^{-3}$ and $\Lambda$ stays constant, so $\Lambda$ increasingly dominates. A flat $\Lambda$-dominated universe approaches $a\propto e^{Ht}$. (Flatness alone does not imply a halt: with $\Lambda=0$ and $\Omega_m=1$ it would, but not here.)

s2-l030-benchmark-model-equality-fate.prompt: Today $\Omega_m\approx0.3$, $\Omega_\Lambda\approx0.7$ and $\Omega_\kappa\approx0$. Looking back to early times (small $a$), which term in $H^2/H_0^2$ is largest?
options: The radiation term $\Omega_ra^{-4}$, because it grows fastest as $a$ shrinks.
The matter term $\Omega_ma^{-3}$, because matter is the most abundant component today.
The cosmological constant $\Omega_\Lambda$, because it is the largest term today.
The curvature term $\Omega_\kappa a^{-2}$, because it dominates whenever $a<1$.
s2-l030-benchmark-model-equality-fate.explanation: Going back in time the terms scale as $a^{-4}>a^{-3}>a^{-2}>a^0$, so radiation always wins at small enough $a$ (before $z\approx3400$), then matter, and only recently $\Lambda$.

s2-l030-benchmark-model-equality-fate.prompt: Describe the order in which radiation, matter and the cosmological constant dominated the energy budget of the universe, and explain why the cosmological constant dominates last.
s2-l030-benchmark-model-equality-fate.rubric: Full credit requires: order radiation -> matter -> Lambda; radiation density falls as a^-4, matter a^-3, Lambda constant; going back in time radiation grows fastest and dominates early; as expansion dilutes both, a constant eventually wins (recently, z ~ 0.3); consequence: expansion becomes exponential and accelerating, fate is eternal expansion.
s2-l030-benchmark-model-equality-fate.modelAnswer: Radiation dominated first, then matter, and now a cosmological constant. Radiation dilutes as $a^{-4}$, matter as $a^{-3}$, and a cosmological constant not at all, so as the universe expands the faster-diluting components fall behind. Once $\Lambda$ wins, the expansion becomes exponential and accelerates, and the universe expands forever.

s2-l031-luminosity-angular-diameter-dist.prompt: The luminosity distance and angular-diameter distance are related by $d_L=(1+z)^2d_A$. What is the main physical origin of this relation?
options: The speed of light changes with redshift, which stretches the distances.
In an expanding universe both distances are tied to the comoving distance $a_0r$.
Light is absorbed by intergalactic dust.
The relation holds only for flat space; curved space gives a different power of $(1+z)$.
s2-l031-luminosity-angular-diameter-dist.explanation: At small $z$, $d_L\approx d_A\approx cz/H_0$. Photon energy and arrival rate each fall by $1/(1+z)$, giving the $(1+z)^2$ flux reduction relative to the geometric $a_0r$.

s2-l031-luminosity-angular-diameter-dist.prompt: A galaxy of fixed physical size is viewed at ever larger redshift, and its angular diameter distance is $d_A=d_L/(1+z)^2$. What does the observed angular size do at very large $z$?
options: It keeps shrinking towards zero, as it would for any object moving farther away.
It stays the same at all redshifts, because angular size depends only on physical size.
It shrinks to zero at the horizon, where $d_A$ diverges because light never arrives.
It stops shrinking and eventually grows again, because $d_A$ reaches a maximum and then decreases.
s2-l031-luminosity-angular-diameter-dist.explanation: In an expanding universe $d_A=a_er$ turns over: light from high-$z$ objects left when the universe was small, so those objects were physically close to us when they emitted. Their angular sizes bottom out near $z\sim1$.

s2-l031-luminosity-angular-diameter-dist.prompt: A supernova has redshift $z=0.050$. For small redshift, $d_L\approx cz/H_0$. Compute its luminosity distance for $H_0=70$ km/s/Mpc, in Mpc.
Explain why the flux from a distant source is reduced by a factor $(1+z)^2$ beyond the ordinary inverse-square dimming with the comoving distance, which leads to $d_L=(1+z)\,a_0r$.
s2-l031-luminosity-angular-diameter-dist.rubric: Full credit requires: each photon loses energy by a factor 1/(1+z) due to the stretching of its wavelength; the photon arrival rate is also reduced by 1/(1+z) because of time dilation of the expansion; together flux is reduced by (1+z)^2 beyond the geometric 1/(4 pi (a0 r)^2).
s2-l031-luminosity-angular-diameter-dist.modelAnswer: Two effects each cost a factor $1/(1+z)$: every photon's energy falls because its wavelength is stretched, and photons arrive less often because the intervals between emissions are stretched too. Together these reduce the flux by $(1+z)^2$ beyond the geometric dilution over the area $4\pi(a_0r)^2$, so $d_L=(1+z)a_0r$.

s2-l032-supernovae-acceleration-vacuum-e.prompt: Distant Type Ia supernovae appeared fainter than expected in a decelerating universe. What did this reveal?
options: They are farther than expected for their redshift.
The supernovae were intrinsically fainter in the past, so nothing was learned.
The universe is contracting.
The speed of light was larger in the past.
s2-l032-supernovae-acceleration-vacuum-e.explanation: Compared with a matter-only universe, acceleration means more time (and distance) elapsed for a given redshift. The 1998 results gave $\Omega_\Lambda\approx0.7$.

s2-l032-supernovae-acceleration-vacuum-e.prompt: A flat universe has $\Omega_m=0.8$ and $\Omega_\Lambda=0.2$. How does its expansion behave today?
options: It is accelerating, because any nonzero $\Omega_\Lambda$ makes the expansion accelerate.
It is still decelerating, because $q_0=0.4-0.2=+0.2>0$.
It is coasting at constant speed, because the two components balance in a flat universe.
It is accelerating, because a flat universe has $q_0<0$ for any matter content.
